title: The three-year cycle
hookLine: Sundays read Matthew, then Mark, then Luke, with John in Lent and Easter
tomorrow: Year two close: the book is a person

cards: Go to Mass in Chicago one Sunday, then fly to Manila and go again the next. The language changes, but the Gospel in Manila picks up right where Chicago's left off, because both parishes are reading from the same plan.

Keep going every Sunday for three years and you'll hear Matthew, Mark and Luke in turn, without anyone choosing a passage on the day. Sunday missals mark the plan with a single capital letter that tells you where you are.

teach.b: The Second Vatican Council asked for the treasures of the Bible to be opened up more lavishly, so that people would hear a fuller share of scripture over a set number of years.
The answer was a new lectionary, the book of readings, issued in 1969. Before it, the Sunday readings came round the same way each year; the new one spread the Sunday Gospels over three years.

teach.h: A IS MATTHEW, B IS MARK, C IS LUKE.
teach.b: Year A reads Matthew, Year B reads Mark, Year C reads Luke.

teach.h: JOHN IN LENT, EASTER AND YEAR B'S SUMMER.
teach.b: John has no year of his own, because he gets the great seasons: much of Lent and Easter in every year, and in Year B, which is short because Mark is short, a run of summer Sundays from John chapter six, the bread of life.
Each Sunday also has an Old Testament reading chosen to echo the Gospel, a Psalm, and a reading from the letters. The weekdays run on a separate two-year cycle for the first reading.
The cycle turns over on the First Sunday of Advent, not on New Year's Day.
The trick for finding the letter: take the calendar year in which the Church's year ends and divide it by three. No remainder means Year C, a remainder of one means A, two means B.
So the year that ends in November 2026 is Year A, Matthew, and Advent 2026 begins Year B.
It reached beyond Catholic churches too: some Protestant churches use the Revised Common Lectionary, which grew out of it, so neighbors down the street may hear the same Gospel on a given Sunday.
And this is the last day of the year of feasts.

how: At Sunday Mass Catholics hear an Old Testament reading, a Psalm, a reading from the letters and a Gospel set by the lectionary's three-year cycle; many missals and apps show the year's letter and the readings for each day.

games.q: you want to know this year's letter. the Church's year ends in 2026. 2026 divided by three leaves a remainder of one. which letter is it?
games.why: a remainder of one means Year A. no remainder means C, and two means B. Advent 2026 begins Year B.

practice: Take the year the Church's current year ends in and divide it by three in your head; take your time.

When you've got the letter, think of its Gospel and one story from it you remember from these two years, a parable, a healing, a meal, and hold that scene as if you were hearing it read aloud on Sunday.
